extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers, peer-review researchers, conference organizers, and authors interested in rebuttal effectiveness
extracted.subtask_description: Study and predict whether a reviewer will increase/decrease/keep her overall score after the rebuttal, and analyze what aspects of reviews, author responses, and peer-review dynamics influence score updates. The paper also presents an ACL-2018 review+rebuttal corpus and qualitative guidance on effective author responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Score (OVAL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall Score OVAL are integers in [1,6]. OVAL is the principal review score used for accept/reject decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OVAL is most strongly correlated with Soundness (SND) and Substance (SBS), followed by Originality (ORG) and Comparison (CMP). Most after-rebuttal changes in OVAL are by one point and concentrate in the borderline area (scores 3–4), where changes can affect acceptance. Predictive models focus on predicting INC/DEC/KEEP for OVAL rather than final accept/reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Confidence (CONF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer Confidence CONF are integer scores in [1,5] indicating the reviewer’s self-assessed confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CONF shows weak positive correlation to Readability (RDB). Features based on CONF did not play a significant role in deciding final score updates in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness (SND)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect score (SND) for soundness, integer in [1,5].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SND is among the strongest correlates of OVAL. Aspect scores like SND change much less often after rebuttal than OVAL; only ~5% of reviews change any aspect score after rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance (SBS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect score (SBS) for substance, integer in [1,5].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SBS is strongly correlated with OVAL; aspect scores rarely change after rebuttal and when they do, they are consistent with OVAL changes (e.g., if OVAL increases, aspects do not decrease).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (ORG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect score (ORG) for originality, integer in [1,5].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ORG is correlated with OVAL but less strongly than SND and SBS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful Comparison (CMP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect score (CMP) for meaningful comparisons to prior work, integer in [1,5].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMP correlates with OVAL; reviewers penalize insufficient comparisons and weak baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability (RDB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect score (RDB) for readability, integer in [1,5].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RDB shows weak correlation with Reviewer Confidence and is one of several aspects considered; poor readability is a common target of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument-based review template (positive/negative arguments and questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to provide positive arguments, negative arguments, and questions; ACL-2018 adopted an argument-based review template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most reviewers used the template: among after-rebuttal reviews, ~80% provide positive arguments, ~82% provide negative arguments, and ~40% provide questions. Counts and lengths of these components were analyzed (e.g., mean lengths: pos arg 22±17 tokens, neg arg 56±53 tokens). A useful review should list concrete positive and negative arguments and explicit questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common weakness type — Evaluation & Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses that criticize Evaluation & Analysis, e.g., lack of error analysis, ablation tests, significance tests, human evaluations, strong baselines, and insufficient (external or internal) comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In manual analysis of ~300 weakness statements this was the most frequent category (~28%). Providing thorough evaluations (ablation, error analysis, significance testing, human evals, strong baselines, adequate comparisons) addresses this common criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common weakness type — Writing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses related to presentation and writing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers frequently criticize poor writing and readability; clearer writing can impact aspect scores and reviewer perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common weakness type — Data issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses concerning data: too few datasets, reliance on English-only or synthetic data, missing agreement scores for new annotations, and non-public resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using multiple and appropriate datasets, reporting annotation agreement, and releasing resources can mitigate these critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common weakness type — Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses pointing to lack of novelty relative to prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly situating contributions and citing recent relevant work helps address novelty concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common weakness type — Motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses concerning insufficient motivation or unclear problem statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better motivation and clear framing of the problem reduce this type of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response quality (subjective 1–10)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subjective perceived quality score for author responses (1 low — 10 high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong responses (scores 8–10) are longer, specific (referring to line numbers/tables), provide numerical values, are detailed and often explain why some criticisms are out-of-scope; weak responses (1–3) are shorter, unspecific, make vague promises (e.g., 'we will try this in the camera-ready'), are off-topic, or apologetic. Politeness alone does not indicate strength; specificity and detailed addressing of reviewer points matter more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response length (log leng)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logarithm of the number of tokens in an author response (used as a feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer author responses tend to be rated higher in quality (mean tokens: weak responses ~53, strong ~90). log leng is among the better non-score features, but correlates with some score features and can be filtered out in feature selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review–response similarity (sim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic similarity between a review and its corresponding response measured by cosine similarity of averaged domain-trained word embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher similarity suggests the response addresses the review (iResps more similar than dResps or kResps). sim is especially predictive for borderline papers: explicit addressing of review points helps increase scores in BRD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity (spec)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-level specificity scores in [0,1] (higher = more specific), computed using a feature-rich model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific responses are judged stronger. Features include max/min/mean/median/std of sentence-level spec. spec and spec-median correlate with INC in borderline cases; unspecific responses are judged weak (vague promises, off-topic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness (plt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-level politeness score (normalized range used in study), quantifying politeness markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politeness has asymmetric effects: being impolite may increase probability of DEC; politeness may help keep a score unchanged but does not strongly increase it for borderline papers. Authors should be polite, but politeness without specificity/convincing content is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincingness (cvc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-level convincingness score (normalized), approximating how convincing individual sentences are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher convincingness (e.g., cvc min/max/median) decreases the probability of DEC and supports INC, especially in borderline submissions. cvc is harder even for humans to judge at sentence level but is predictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer pressure / gap-to-peers features
rubrics_metrics.description: Features reflecting the gap between a reviewer’s initial score and other reviewers’ scores (e.g., oth_mean-self, self-oth_min).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features are the strongest predictors of score changes: reviewers tend to move toward the mean of peers. Large positive gap (others' mean above self) strongly increases probability of INC; large negative gap increases probability of DEC. The study calls this conformity bias or 'peer pressure' and finds it to be the dominant factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal phase influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The rebuttal phase has a marginal but statistically significant influence on final scores; this influence is stronger for borderline papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although rebuttals can change final OVALs and thereby affect acceptance rates, the overall effect size is small compared to peer pressure. Papers with at least one INC review have much higher acceptance rates (~49.8%) than those with at least one DEC (~7.2%) or no update (~22.8%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect scores rarely change after rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: After rebuttal, changes to individual aspect scores (SND, SBS, ORG, CMP, RDB) are uncommon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only ~5% of reviews change any aspect score after rebuttal; only ~1% change confidence. Aspect score changes are consistent with OVAL changes (no aspect decreases when OVAL increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission timing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing of review submission relative to the deadline (submission time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 51.6% of reviews submitted within the last 3 days before the deadline. Mean submission time for INC reviews is ~20 hours earlier than for DEC reviews (p=0.009). Submission time is weakly positively correlated with initial score: early submitters have slightly lower initial scores and may be more likely to increase later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-based features matter more for borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual features (spec, sim, cvc) are more predictive for the Borderline Submissions (BRD) subset than for the Full set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For BRD, weights for cvc_min, spec_median and sim are relatively high (>0.2) in predicting INC. This suggests reviewers pay more attention to specificity, explicit addressing, and convincingness when the decision is close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness asymmetry in effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Politeness features have asymmetric effects: politeness may prevent a score decrease but does not reliably cause increases for borderline papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Full models politeness (plt_max) helps increase OVAL (positive weight for INC); in BRD, plt_max is predictive of KEEP rather than INC, and plt_max is the second-best text feature for predicting DEC in BRD (negative weight for DEC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural recommendation to reduce conformity bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested procedure: blind reviewers from each other during rebuttal updates, allowing updates only based on author responses; area chairs see all reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinding reviewers to peer reviews (only showing authors' responses) may reduce conformity and make rebuttal updates more directly responsive to author-provided evidence/arguments rather than peer opinions. This is proposed as a practical mitigation for conformity bias observed in the study.
